cse-2025-2-cs-30.approach: Only two items can clash: the reduction $A \to d\cdot$ sits next to a shift in two different states. Compare SLR look-aheads (FOLLOW$(A)$) with LR(1) look-aheads in those two states, then check whether LALR merging changes anything.
cse-2025-2-cs-30.given: Augmented grammar: $S' \to S$, $S \to Aa \mid bAc \mid dc \mid bda$, $A \to d$.

steps.title: FOLLOW(A) for SLR
steps.body: $A$ appears in $S \to A\,a$ (followed by $a$) and $S \to b\,A\,c$ (followed by $c$). So $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a, c\}$. An SLR parser reduces $A \to d$ on **both** $a$ and $c$ in every state containing $A \to d\cdot$.

steps.title: State reached on d from the start
steps.body:
From $I_0$ on $d$: $I_d = \{\, S \to d\cdot c,\ \ A \to d\cdot \,\}$.

- SLR: shift on $c$ (from $S \to d\cdot c$) **and** reduce on $c \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ → **S/R conflict**.
- LR(1): in $I_0$ the item $A \to \cdot d$ comes only from $S \to \cdot A a$, so its look-ahead is $\{a\}$. Reduce on $a$, shift on $c$ → no conflict.

steps.title: State reached on b then d
steps.body:
From $I_0$ on $b$: $\{S \to b\cdot Ac,\ S \to b\cdot da,\ A \to \cdot d\}$; then on $d$: $I_{bd} = \{\, S \to bd\cdot a,\ \ A \to d\cdot \,\}$.

- SLR: shift on $a$ and reduce on $a \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ → **S/R conflict**.
- LR(1): here $A \to \cdot d$ came from $S \to b\cdot Ac$, so its look-ahead is $\{c\}$. Shift on $a$, reduce on $c$ → no conflict.

steps.title: LALR merging changes nothing
steps.body:
LALR merges only LR(1) states with the **same core**. The two states holding $A \to d\cdot$ have different cores ($\{S \to d\cdot c, A \to d\cdot\}$ vs $\{S \to bd\cdot a, A \to d\cdot\}$), and every other state has a unique core. So the LALR(1) table equals the CLR(1) table and is conflict-free.

Hence $G$ is **LALR(1) (and CLR(1)) but not SLR(1)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: LALR(1) succeeds: the only reduce states have distinct cores, so no merging and no conflict.
There is nothing to separate CLR(1) from LALR(1) here — no two LR(1) states share a core, so the tables coincide.
LR(1)/LALR(1) look-aheads ($\{a\}$ and $\{c\}$) avoid the clashes, but FOLLOW$(A)=\{a,c\}$ gives S/R conflicts in two SLR states.
SLR(1) fails: with FOLLOW$(A)=\{a,c\}$, state $\{S\to d\cdot c, A\to d\cdot\}$ conflicts on $c$ (and $\{S\to bd\cdot a, A\to d\cdot\}$ on $a$).

cse-2025-2-cs-30.shortcut: This is the textbook "LALR but not SLR" pattern: the same reduction $A\to d$ is followed by $a$ in one context and $c$ in the other, and each context also has a shift on the *other* symbol. FOLLOW mixes the two contexts; LR(1) keeps them apart, and the cores differ so LALR does too.
pitfalls: Assuming any grammar that is not SLR(1) must fail LALR(1) too.
Thinking LALR merging always introduces conflicts — it only merges states with identical cores.
Forgetting to check both states that contain $A \to d\cdot$.
cse-2025-2-cs-30.verification: Parse $da$: after $d$ with look-ahead $a$, LR(1) reduces $A\to d$, then shifts $a$, reduces $S\to Aa$ ✓. Parse $dc$: look-ahead $c$ → shift, reduce $S\to dc$ ✓. The SLR parser cannot decide on $c$ in that same state.

cse-2025-2-cs-31.approach: Find the peak with a binary search on the slope ($A[m]$ vs $A[m+1]$), then binary-search the increasing part and the decreasing part. Three $O(\log n)$ searches give $O(\log n)$, and a sorted array (a special bitonic array) already forces $\Omega(\log n)$.

steps.title: Find the peak in O(log n)
steps.body:
Compare $A[m]$ with $A[m+1]$: if $A[m] < A[m+1]$ we are on the rising slope, so the peak is right of $m$; otherwise it is at $m$ or left of it. Each probe halves the range (distinct elements make the test unambiguous): $O(\log n)$ comparisons.

Example $A = [2,5,9,14,11,7,3]$: $m=3$: $14 > 11$ → go left; $m=1$: $5 < 9$ → go right; $m=2$: $9<14$ → peak at index 3.

steps.title: Two ordinary binary searches
steps.body:
The prefix $A[1..i]$ is ascending and the suffix $A[i+1..n]$ is descending, so search each with binary search: $O(\log n) + O(\log n)$.

Example, key $7$: not in $[2,5,9,14]$; in the descending part $[11,7,3]$ the middle element is $7$ → found.

Total: $3 \cdot O(\log n) = O(\log n)$.

steps.title: Lower bound Ω(log n)
steps.body: A fully sorted array is bitonic (take $i = n$). Any comparison-based search in a sorted array of $n$ elements needs $\Omega(\log n)$ comparisons (a decision tree with $n+1$ outcomes has depth $\ge \log_2(n+1)$). Hence the best bound is $\Theta(\log n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Linear scan works but is not the best possible: the peak plus two binary searches use only $O(\log n)$ comparisons.
Impossible: even a sorted array needs $\Omega(\log n)$ comparisons.
$\Theta(\log^2 n)$ is what a careless nested search would give; three sequential binary searches add up to $O(\log n)$, not multiply.
Upper bound $O(\log n)$ (peak + two binary searches) matches the $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound from sorted arrays.

cse-2025-2-cs-31.shortcut: Sorted arrays are a special case → at least $\log n$; peak finding + 2 binary searches → at most $3\log n$. So $\Theta(\log n)$.
pitfalls: Reading option (C) as $\log_2 n$ — it is $\log^2 n$.
Multiplying the costs of the peak search and the binary searches instead of adding them.
cse-2025-2-cs-31.verification: For $n = 2^{20}$: about 20 probes for the peak and at most 20 + 20 for the two halves — 60 comparisons, i.e. a constant times $\log n$.

cse-2025-2-cs-32.approach: Identify each $f$ with the bit-vector $(f(1),\dots,f(n))$, i.e. a subset of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Then $f \preccurlyeq g$ is exactly subset inclusion, so $(\mathcal F,\preccurlyeq)$ is the Boolean lattice $2^n$.

steps.title: Partial order
steps.body:
- Reflexive: $f(x) \le f(x)$ for all $x$.
- Antisymmetric: $f \preccurlyeq g$ and $g \preccurlyeq f$ give $f(x)=g(x)$ for all $x$, so $f = g$.
- Transitive: $f(x) \le g(x) \le h(x)$ gives $f(x) \le h(x)$.

So (B) is true.

steps.title: Lattice
steps.body: For any $f, g$: $(f \wedge g)(x) = \min(f(x), g(x))$ is the greatest lower bound and $(f \vee g)(x) = \max(f(x), g(x))$ is the least upper bound — both are again functions to $\{0,1\}$. Every pair has a meet and a join, so (C) is true (it is the Boolean lattice, isomorphic to $(2^{\{1..n\}}, \subseteq)$).

steps.title: Not symmetric, so not an equivalence
steps.body:
Take $f \equiv 0$ and $g \equiv 1$: $f \preccurlyeq g$ but $g 
ot\preccurlyeq f$ (since $1 
ot\le 0$). So $\preccurlyeq$ is not symmetric (A false) and therefore not an equivalence relation (D false). (Here $n \ge 1$, so such $f 
e g$ exist.)

optionAnalysis.reason: $0 \preccurlyeq 1$ (constant functions) but not $1 \preccurlyeq 0$.
Pointwise $\le$ inherits reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity from $\le$ on $\{0,1\}$.
Pointwise min and max are the meet and join; it is the Boolean lattice $2^n$.
An equivalence relation must be symmetric, which fails.

cse-2025-2-cs-32.shortcut: Functions $\{1..n\}\to\{0,1\}$ = subsets of $\{1..n\}$, and $\preccurlyeq$ = $\subseteq$. Subset inclusion is the classic lattice and is never symmetric.
pitfalls: Confusing antisymmetric with "not symmetric" — the relation is antisymmetric, which is exactly why it is a partial order.
Thinking a partial order that is not total cannot be a lattice.
cse-2025-2-cs-32.verification: Hasse diagram for $n=2$ (right): a diamond, the smallest non-chain lattice; $01$ and $10$ are incomparable yet have meet $00$ and join $11$.

cse-2025-2-cs-33.approach: Read the map (rows $wx$, columns $yz$ in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10): the four corners and the central $2\times2$ block are 1. So $F = \bar x\bar z + xz$; then test each option by listing exactly which cells it covers.

steps.title: Read the minimal expression
steps.body:
Corners: $x = 0, z = 0$ with $w, y$ free → $\bar x \bar z$ (minterms $0, 2, 8, 10$).
Centre block: rows $wx = 01, 11$ and columns $yz = 01, 11$ → $x = 1, z = 1$ → $xz$ (minterms $5, 7, 13, 15$).

$$F = \bar x\bar z + xz \quad(= \overline{x \oplus z})$$

So (D) is correct.

steps.title: Option (A)
steps.body: $\bar w\bar x\bar y\bar z = m_0$, $w\bar x\bar y\bar z = m_8$, $\bar w\bar x y\bar z = m_2$, $w\bar x y\bar z = m_{10}$: exactly the four corners, i.e. $\bar x\bar z$ written as minterms. Plus $xz$. Equals $F$ ✓.

steps.title: Option (B)
steps.body: Terms: $m_0$, $m_2$, $w\bar x yz = m_{11}$, and $xz$. It misses $m_8$, $m_{10}$ (corners that are 1) and includes $m_{11}$ (row $wx=10$, column $yz=11$), which is **0** in the map ✗.

steps.title: Option (C)
steps.body: Terms: $m_0$, $m_8$, $w\bar x\bar y z = m_9$, and $xz$. It misses $m_2$, $m_{10}$ and includes $m_9$ (row $10$, column $01$), which is **0** ✗.

optionAnalysis.reason: Its four minterms are exactly the four corner 1s ($\bar x\bar z$, unminimised), plus $xz$.
Contains $w\bar x yz$ ($m_{11}$), a 0-cell, and misses the corners $m_8$, $m_{10}$.
Contains $w\bar x\bar y z$ ($m_9$), a 0-cell, and misses $m_2$, $m_{10}$.
The minimal SOP: corner quad $\bar x\bar z$ plus centre quad $xz$.

cse-2025-2-cs-33.shortcut: Every term with $\bar x$ must also have $\bar z$ (the 1s with $x=0$ are exactly the $z=0$ cells). (B) has $w\bar x yz$ and (C) has $w\bar x\bar y z$, both with $\bar x z$ → wrong.
pitfalls: Missing the four-corner wrap-around group.
Accepting an expression because it "contains $xz$" without checking that its extra terms stay inside the 1s.
cse-2025-2-cs-33.verification: Count: $F$ has 8 ones. (A) covers 4 + 4 = 8 distinct cells, all 1s; (D) also 8. (B) and (C) each cover a 0-cell.

cse-2025-2-cs-34.approach: Use $\det P = \det L \cdot \det U$ with $\det L = 1$ (unit lower triangular) and $\det U = u_{11}u_{22}u_{33}$; test (D) with a small symmetric counterexample.

steps.title: (A) forward then back substitution
steps.body: $PX = Q \iff L(UX) = Q$. Put $Y = UX$: solve $LY = Q$ by forward substitution, then $UX = Y$ by back substitution. This is exactly how LU is used ✓.

steps.title: Determinants give (B) and (C)
steps.body:
$\det L = 1\cdot1\cdot1 = 1$ and $\det U = u_{11}u_{22}u_{33}$, so

$$\det P = \det L \cdot \det U = u_{11}u_{22}u_{33}.$$

- (B): $P$ invertible ⇒ $\det P \ne 0$ ⇒ $\det U \ne 0$; and $L$ is always invertible ($\det L = 1$) ✓.
- (C): $P$ singular ⇒ $u_{11}u_{22}u_{33} = 0$ ⇒ some $u_{ii} = 0$ ✓.

steps.title: (D) fails: counterexample
steps.body:
$P = \begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\2&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$ is symmetric. Elimination ($R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$) gives

$L = \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$, $U = \begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&-3&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.

Neither is symmetric. In fact a triangular matrix is symmetric only if it is diagonal, and a unit lower-triangular diagonal matrix is $I$ — so (D) would force $P$ to be diagonal ✗.

optionAnalysis.reason: Standard use of LU: forward substitution for $LY=Q$, back substitution for $UX=Y$.
$\det L = 1$ always; $\det U = \det P \ne 0$.
$0 = \det P = u_{11}u_{22}u_{33}$, so some diagonal entry of $U$ is 0.
For symmetric $P$ one gets $P = LDL^T$ ($U = DL^T$), not symmetric $L, U$; the $3\times3$ counterexample above shows it.

cse-2025-2-cs-34.shortcut: Remember $\det P = \prod u_{ii}$ (because $\det L = 1$): that settles (B) and (C) at once. A symmetric triangular matrix must be diagonal, so (D) is absurd in general.
pitfalls: Confusing symmetric $P = LDL^T$ (Cholesky-like) with "L and U symmetric".
Forgetting that $L$ has unit diagonal, hence is always invertible.

cse-2025-2-cs-35.approach: Ask, for each scheme, what happens on PUSH and especially on POP of the current minimum. Only a per-record "minimum so far" pointer keeps MIN, PUSH and POP all $O(1)$.

steps.title: (A) min pointer stored in every record
steps.body:
On PUSH($r$): $r$.minptr $=$ the record with smaller key among $r$ and top.minptr (one comparison, $O(1)$). MIN returns top.minptr in $O(1)$. On POP the record below already stores the minimum of the remaining stack — nothing to recompute. All $O(1)$ ✓.

(The question says "smallest key below it"; whether or not the record itself is included, MIN = min(top, top.ptr) is still one comparison.)

scene.caption: push 7, 3, 9, 1 — each record stores the min below/including it

steps.title: POP keeps MIN correct for (A), breaks (B)
steps.body:
POP removes $1$; the new top $9$ stores $↓3$, so MIN $= 3$ instantly.

(B) keeps a single global pointer. After popping the minimum record that pointer is useless, and finding the new minimum requires scanning the stack — $O(n)$, so POP (or MIN) becomes $O(n)$ ✗.

steps.title: (C) and (D) slow down PUSH/POP
steps.body:
- (C) sorted auxiliary array: PUSH must insert the key in order — $O(n)$ shifts (and POP must delete an arbitrary key, $O(n)$) ✗.
- (D) min-heap: MIN is $O(1)$, but PUSH becomes heap-insert $O(\log n)$ and POP must delete an arbitrary key from the heap, $O(\log n)$ — the standard $O(1)$ stack operations get slower ✗.

optionAnalysis.reason: Each record carries the minimum of the stack beneath it; PUSH is one comparison, POP restores the old minimum automatically, MIN is $O(1)$.
Works for PUSH, but after POPping the minimum the new minimum must be searched for in $O(n)$.
Keeping a sorted array costs $O(n)$ per PUSH/POP (insertion/deletion with shifting).
Heap insert/delete cost $O(\log n)$, so PUSH and POP are no longer $O(1)$.

cse-2025-2-cs-35.shortcut: A stack only ever removes the newest element, so "the minimum at the time each record was pushed" is all you need — store it with the record.
pitfalls: Choosing (B) because it handles PUSH and MIN, forgetting POP of the minimum.
Accepting (D) because MIN is $O(1)$ — the condition is that PUSH/POP must stay $O(1)$ too.
cse-2025-2-cs-35.verification: Pop all four records one by one: the MIN values read from the new tops are $3, 3, 7$ and then empty — matching a brute-force scan of $\{7,3,9\}, \{7,3\}, \{7\}$.

cse-2025-2-cs-36.approach: Find each relation's candidate keys (attributes never on a right-hand side must be in every key), then test every FD with the 3NF rule: LHS is a superkey, or every RHS attribute is prime.

steps.title: R1: key is AD
steps.body:
Right-hand sides: $E, B, C$. So $A$ and $D$ are in every key.

$\{A,D\}^+ = \{A,D\} \xrightarrow{D\to E} \{A,D,E\} \xrightarrow{EA\to B} \{A,B,D,E\} \xrightarrow{EB\to C} \{A,B,C,D,E\}$.

Only candidate key: $AD$. Prime attributes: $A, D$.

steps.title: R1 violates 3NF
steps.body: $D \to E$: $D^+ = \{D, E\}$, so $D$ is not a superkey, and $E$ is not prime ⇒ **violation** (a partial dependency on part of the key). R1 is NOT in 3NF (also $EA\to B$ and $EB\to C$ violate).

steps.title: R2: key is C
steps.body:
Right-hand sides: $D, B, A$. So $C$ is in every key.

$C^+ = \{C\} \xrightarrow{C\to A} \{A,C\} \xrightarrow{A\to D,\ A\to B} \{A,B,C,D\}$.

Only candidate key: $C$. Prime attribute: $C$ only.

steps.title: R2 violates 3NF
steps.body: $A \to D$: $A^+ = \{A, B, D\}$ is not a superkey and $D$ is not prime ⇒ **violation** (transitive dependency $C \to A \to D$). Same for $A \to B$. R2 is NOT in 3NF.

answer.value: **(C) and (D)** — neither R1 nor R2 is in 3NF

optionAnalysis.reason: $D \to E$ has a non-superkey LHS and a non-prime RHS (key is $AD$).
$A \to D$ (and $A \to B$) has a non-superkey LHS and a non-prime RHS (key is $C$).
R1 has the partial dependency $D \to E$ on its key $AD$.
R2 has the transitive dependency $C \to A \to D$.

cse-2025-2-cs-36.shortcut: Options (A)/(C) and (B)/(D) are complementary pairs, so exactly one of each pair is true. One violating FD per relation ($D\to E$, $A\to D$) decides both.
pitfalls: Missing that $A$ must be part of R1's key (it never appears on a RHS).
Thinking $A$ is a key of R2 — $A^+$ lacks $C$.
cse-2025-2-cs-36.verification: Brute force: no proper subset of $AD$ determines $C$ ($A^+ = \{A\}$, $D^+ = \{D,E\}$), and only sets containing $C$ determine $C$ in R2, so the keys are right and the violations stand.

cse-2025-2-cs-37.approach: Check each replacement (refs 4, 5, 6, 1, 3, 2) against each policy's rule. One contradiction kills a policy; OPT fits every replacement (with the remaining ties broken by load order).
cse-2025-2-cs-37.given: Victims read from the table: ref 4 evicts **2**, ref 5 evicts **3**, ref 6 evicts **1**, ref 1 evicts **4**, ref 3 evicts **5**, ref 2 evicts **6**. Faults: 9 (3 cold + 6 replacements).

steps.title: LRU fails at the first replacement
steps.body: At ref 4 the frames hold $\{1,2,3\}$, last used at times 1, 2, 3. LRU evicts **1**, but the table evicts **2** ✗. (Run to the end, LRU gives 11 faults, not 9.)

scene.caption: LRU evicts 1 here — the table evicts 2

steps.title: LFU fails at ref 6
steps.body: Before ref 6 the frames are $\{1,4,5\}$ with use counts $1{:}\,2$ (refs 1, 7), $4{:}\,2$ (refs 4, 6), $5{:}\,1$. LFU must evict **5**, but the table evicts **1** ✗.

steps.title: MFU fails too
steps.body: At ref 4 and at ref 5 every resident page has been used exactly once, so MFU has only ties — and the table evicts the *middle* page each time (2 out of 1,2,3; then 3 out of 1,4,3). A FIFO/LRU tie rule would evict 1, an MRU rule 3 and then 4: no fixed rule gives 2 and then 3. Moreover, if counts survive eviction, page 1 has 3 references at ref 3 and MFU would evict 1, not 5 ✗. Only case-by-case tie-breaking could mimic the table, which is not a policy.

steps.title: OPT explains every replacement
steps.body:
Next uses after each fault:

| ref | frames | next use | victim |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 1,2,3 | 1→7th, 2→13th, 3→12th | **2** ✓ |
| 5 | 1,4,3 | 1→7th, 4→6th, 3→12th | **3** ✓ |
| 6 | 1,4,5 | 4→9th, 5→10th, 1→11th | **1** ✓ |
| 1 | 6,4,5 | none used again | **4** (tie) ✓ |
| 3 | 6,1,5 | none used again | **5** (tie) ✓ |
| 2 | 6,1,3 | none | **6** (tie) ✓ |

Every forced choice matches, and the ties are resolved by evicting the earliest-loaded page. 9 faults.

optionAnalysis.reason: At ref 4 LRU would evict page 1 (least recently used), the table evicts 2.
At ref 6 page 5 has the lowest count (1) but page 1 (count 2) is evicted.
At refs 4 and 5 all counts are equal and the middle page is evicted (2, then 3) — no MFU tie rule does that; with persistent counts it would also evict page 1, not 5, at ref 3.
Each forced choice evicts the page used farthest in the future (2, 3, 1); the rest are ties among pages never used again.

cse-2025-2-cs-37.shortcut: The first replacement alone is decisive: at ref 4, page 2 is evicted although page 1 is the oldest and least recent — only "farthest next use" (2 at position 13) explains it.
pitfalls: Treating the cold misses 1*, 2*, 3* as replacements.
Ignoring tie situations when ruling a policy in — OPT's later victims are ties and are all legal.
cse-2025-2-cs-37.verification: Simulating OPT (ties → earliest loaded) on the 13 references reproduces every column of the table and 9 faults; LRU gives 11.

cse-2025-2-cs-38.approach: With single-instance resources, deadlock ⇔ a cycle in the wait-for graph. Collapse the RAG to a wait-for graph, list its cycles, and check which abort set hits every cycle.

steps.title: Two cycles
steps.body:
Cycle 1: $P_1 \to P_2 \to P_3 \to P_1$ (through $R_2, R_3, R_1$).
Cycle 2: $P_2 \to P_4 \to P_2$ (through $R_4, R_2$).

The system is deadlocked; an abort set works iff it contains a process of **both** cycles. $P_2$ is on both.

steps.title: Abort P1 or P3: cycle 2 survives
steps.body: Removing $P_1$ (or $P_3$) breaks cycle 1 only; $P_2 \to R_4 \to P_4 \to R_2 \to P_2$ is still a cycle ⇒ still deadlocked. (A), (B) false.

steps.title: Abort P2, or P1 and P4: deadlock free
steps.body:
- Abort $P_2$: $R_2$ is released and both cycles disappear (each passes through $P_2$) ✓.
- Abort $P_1$ and $P_4$: cycle 1 loses $P_1$, cycle 2 loses $P_4$. Remaining waits $P_2 \to P_3$ only; $P_3$ can get $R_1$ (freed by $P_1$), finish, release $R_3$, then $P_2$ gets $R_3, R_4$ ✓.

scene.caption: abort P2: every cycle is broken

optionAnalysis.reason: Breaks $P_1\to P_2\to P_3\to P_1$ but leaves $P_2 \leftrightarrow P_4$ deadlocked.
Same as (A): cycle $P_2 \to P_4 \to P_2$ remains.
$P_2$ lies on both cycles; aborting it frees $R_2$ and removes every cycle.
$P_1$ hits the first cycle and $P_4$ the second; what remains is acyclic.

cse-2025-2-cs-38.shortcut: Find the process common to all cycles ($P_2$) — any abort set must contain it or one member of each cycle; $\{P_1, P_4\}$ is such a hitting set.
pitfalls: Missing the second (two-process) cycle $P_2 \leftrightarrow P_4$ because $P_2$ has two outgoing claim edges.
Reading "claim edge" in the Banker's sense — here it is defined as an actual wait (request) edge.
cse-2025-2-cs-38.verification: After aborting $P_2$: waits are $P_1 \to R_2$ (free), $P_3 \to R_1$ (held by $P_1$), $P_4 \to R_2$ (free): $P_1$ and $P_4$ can proceed, then $P_3$ — no cycle.

cse-2025-2-cs-39.approach: Decode the three words (sign | 8-bit exponent with bias 127 | fraction). The fractions have only one or three leading bits, so each value is a small integer; then evaluate the four equations.

steps.title: Decode RY and RZ
steps.body:
RY = 0x40C00000 = `0 10000001 1000…`: exponent $129 \Rightarrow 2^2$, significand $1.1_2 = 1.5$, so $Y = 1.5 \times 4 = 6$.

RZ = 0x41400000 = `0 10000010 1000…`: exponent $130 \Rightarrow 2^3$, significand $1.5$, so $Z = 1.5 \times 8 = 12$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $-9+6+12 = 9$; it would be 0 only if the sign bit of RX were misread (e.g. $X=-18$) or the bias wrong.

cse-2025-2-cs-39.shortcut: Hex digit after the sign/exponent nibbles: 0x41 4… means exponent 130 and fraction .1 → $1.5\times 8 = 12$; 0x40C… → $1.5\times4 = 6$; 0xC11… → $-1.125\times8 = -9$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the hidden leading 1 (giving $X = -1$, $Y = 2$, $Z = 4$).
Using bias 128 instead of 127, which halves every value.

cse-2025-2-cs-40.approach: Compare minterm sets for (A); use the consensus theorem for (B) and (C); push the complement through the product with De Morgan for (D).

steps.title: (A): compare minterms
steps.body:
LHS (order $ABC$): $\bar ABC = m_3$, $A\bar B\bar C = m_4$, $\bar A\bar B\bar C = m_0$, $A\bar BC = m_5$, $ABC = m_7$ → $\{0,3,4,5,7\}$.

RHS: $BC = \{3,7\}$, $\bar B\bar C = \{0,4\}$, $\bar A\bar B = \{0,1\}$ → $\{0,1,3,4,7\}$.

They differ at $m_1$ and $m_5$ (e.g. $A=1,B=0,C=1$: LHS $=1$, RHS $=0$) ✗.

steps.title: (B): consensus theorem
steps.body:
$BC$ is the consensus of $AB$ and $\bar AC$:

$BC = BC(A + \bar A) = ABC + \bar ABC$, and $ABC$ is absorbed by $AB$, $\bar ABC$ by $\bar AC$. So $AB + \bar AC + BC = AB + \bar AC$ ✓.

steps.title: (C): expand the product
steps.body: $(A+C)(\bar A+B) = A\bar A + AB + \bar AC + BC = AB + \bar AC + BC$ (since $A\bar A = 0$) $= AB + \bar AC$ by (B) ✓.

steps.title: (D): De Morgan
steps.body:
The complement of a product is the sum of the complemented factors:

$\overline{(A+\bar B+\bar D)} = \bar A B D$, $\overline{(C+D)} = \bar C\bar D$, $\overline{(\bar A+C+D)} = A\bar C\bar D$, $\overline{(A+B+\bar D)} = \bar A\bar B D$.

Sum: $\bar ABD + \bar A\bar BD + \bar C\bar D + A\bar C\bar D = \bar AD(B+\bar B) + \bar C\bar D(1 + A) = \bar AD + \bar C\bar D$ ✓.

optionAnalysis.reason: LHS has $m_5$ ($A\bar BC$) but not $m_1$; RHS has $m_1$ ($\bar A\bar B$ with $C=1$) but not $m_5$.
Consensus theorem: $BC$ is redundant.
Expanding gives $AB + \bar AC + BC$, which reduces to $AB + \bar AC$ by consensus.
De Morgan turns the complemented product into $\bar ABD + \bar C\bar D + A\bar C\bar D + \bar A\bar BD = \bar AD + \bar C\bar D$.

cse-2025-2-cs-40.shortcut: (B) and (C) are the consensus theorem and its dual form; (A) fails on the single input $A=1, B=0, C=1$.
pitfalls: Missing that the overbar in (D) spans the whole product (it is not four separate complemented sums).
Comparing (A) term-by-term instead of by minterm sets.
cse-2025-2-cs-40.verification: Spot-check (D) at $A=0,B=0,C=1,D=1$: factors $= (0+1+0)(1)(1)(0+0+0) = 0$, complement $= 1$; RHS $\bar AD = 1$ ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-41.approach: Show both grammars are ambiguous by exhibiting two parse trees for one string; an ambiguous grammar is never LL(1). (G1 is the classic dangling-else grammar; G2 only looks like the textbook fix.)

steps.title: G1 is ambiguous
steps.body: `if b then if b then a else a` has two trees: the `else` belongs to the inner `if` ($S \to$ if $E$ then $S$ with inner $S \to$ if $E$ then $S$ else $S$), or to the outer one ($S \to$ if $E$ then $S$ else $S$ with inner $S \to$ if $E$ then $S$). So G1 is ambiguous and not LL(1) (it also has two $S$-productions starting with `if`, a FIRST/FIRST clash).

steps.title: G2 is ambiguous too
steps.body:
In G2 the else-part of $M$ is an $S$, which may be an unmatched `if`. Take

`if b then if b then c else if b then c else c`.

**Tree 1:** outer $S \to$ if $E$ then $S$ (unmatched); inner $S \Rightarrow M \to$ if $E$ then $M$ else $S$ with $M\Rightarrow c$ and the else-part $S \Rightarrow M \to$ if $E$ then $c$ else $c$. The 1st `else` goes to the 2nd `if`, the 2nd `else` to the 3rd `if`.

steps.title: Second parse tree
steps.body:
**Tree 2:** $S \Rightarrow M \to$ if $E$ then $M_1$ else $S$ with final $S \Rightarrow c$, where $M_1 \to$ if $E$ then $M$ else $S$ = `if b then c else if b then c` (the else-part $S \to$ if $E$ then $S$ is unmatched, which $M$ allows). Now the 2nd `else` goes to the **1st** `if`.

Two distinct leftmost derivations ⇒ G2 is ambiguous.

steps.title: Neither is LL(1)
steps.body: An ambiguous grammar is never LL(1). Directly for G2: $S \to$ if $E$ then $S$ and $S \to M$ with $\text{FIRST}(M) = \{\text{if}, c\}$ — both alternatives can start with `if`, so the LL(1) table cell $[S, \text{if}]$ has two entries. Hence (C) and (D) are true; (A) and (B) false.

optionAnalysis.reason: G2 is not LL(1): $S \to$ if… and $S \to M$ both start with `if` (and G2 is ambiguous).
G1 is the dangling-else grammar — ambiguous and with a FIRST/FIRST clash, so not LL(1).
Both have FIRST/FIRST conflicts on `if` and both are ambiguous.
Two parse trees: `if b then if b then a else a` for G1, `if b then if b then c else if b then c else c` for G2.

cse-2025-2-cs-41.shortcut: Both grammars have two $S$-alternatives that can begin with `if`, so neither is LL(1) — that settles (A), (B), (C). For (D), remember that the correct matched/unmatched grammar needs the then-part *and* the else-part of a matched statement to be matched; G2 allows an unmatched else-part.
pitfalls: Assuming G2 is the textbook unambiguous dangling-else fix — the else-branch of $M$ is $S$, not $M$.
Thinking left factoring G1 makes it unambiguous — it remains ambiguous.
cse-2025-2-cs-41.verification: Count the `else`s in the two G2 trees: tree 1 pairs (if₂, else₁), (if₃, else₂); tree 2 pairs (if₂, else₁), (if₁, else₂) — different structures for the same token string.

animation.title: G2: two parse trees for if b then if b then c else if b then c else c

cse-2025-2-cs-42.approach: Simplify each set first. (A) is a regular expression, (C) is a product of two modular counters, while (B) and (D) reduce to an equal-count language $a^nb^n$ (possibly restricted), which needs unbounded memory.

steps.title: (A) and (C) are regular
steps.body:
(A) $\{a^mb^n\} = a^*b^*$, a regular expression ✓.

(C) Track $\#_a \bmod 7$ and $\#_b \bmod 9$: a product DFA with $7 \times 9 = 63$ states, accepting the single state $(2, 3)$ ✓.

steps.title: (B) collapses to aⁿbⁿ
steps.body: Words in $\{a,b\}^*$ contain no $c$, so we need $m - n = 0$. With $m \ge n \ge 0$ that leaves $\{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 0\}$, the standard non-regular language (pumping $a^pb^p$ inside the first $p$ symbols changes only the $a$-count) ✗.

steps.title: (D) is not regular
steps.body: Suppose $L_D$ were regular. Then $L_D \cap a^*b^* = \{a^nb^n \mid n \equiv 2 \pmod 7\}$ would be regular. But the prefixes $a^{7i+2}$ ($i = 0,1,2,\dots$) are pairwise distinguishable: $a^{7i+2}b^{7i+2}$ is in the language while $a^{7j+2}b^{7i+2}$ ($j \ne i$) is not. Infinitely many Myhill–Nerode classes ⇒ not regular ✗.

optionAnalysis.reason: It is $a^*b^*$.
Intersecting with $\{a,b\}^*$ forces $m = n$, giving $\{a^nb^n\}$.
Two independent bounded counters: a 63-state product DFA.
The condition $\#_a = \#_b$ is unbounded; the mod-7 restriction does not make it finite-state.

cse-2025-2-cs-42.shortcut: Bounded counting (mod $k$) is regular; comparing two unbounded counts ($\#_a = \#_b$, $a^nb^n$) is not — even when intersected with a regular condition.
pitfalls: Thinking the regular intersection in (B) or the mod condition in (D) "tames" the language.
Confusing (C) with (D): (C) never compares $a$ with $b$.
cse-2025-2-cs-42.verification: Sanity: (D) contains $a^2b^2$, $a^9b^9$, $a^{16}b^{16}, \dots$ — a DFA would have to remember $\#_a - \#_b$ exactly, which is unbounded.
